newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury says bank plan to keep thrift powers.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury says bank plan to keep thrift powers.

text.p: The Treasury's plan on merging the thrift and bank industry charters will not eliminate the powers that thrifts currently have, and will broaden the powers for banks, Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke said Wednesday.

"We want to take the best of both," Hawke told Reuters in a telephone interview. "We want to be able to accommodate all of those institutions that are presently operating as thrifts, but ... to do it under a bank charter that would be broad enough to accommodate all of the things that they are presently doing," he said.

Treasury is required to put forth its plan on merging the charters by March 31, 1997. Hawke said an outline of that proposal would be issued earlier than the deadline and it would include the wider issue of how to tear down the Depression-era Glass-Steagall law.
While Treasury has not firmed up how far it will propose to go on the question of what entities banks should be allowed to affiliate with, it supported broad affiliation, he said.
The plan that Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, R-NY, proposed in the past Congressional session has "great appeal," Hawke said.
D'Amato had proposed allowing banks to affiliate with insurance, securities and commercial companies.

"Our present thinking is that there ought to be broad latitude for banking organizations to engage in activities that are financially related under some broad standard and to affiliate with a wide range of organizations," Hawke said.
"I don't know how far we will go on the affiliations question," he added.

The Treasury's plan might limit what banks can do through their own subsidiaries "to a broad array of financially related services which would include insurance and securities activities, we might be even broader than that at the holding company level," Hawke said.
A key factor in the past that held up Glass-Steagall reform was heavy opposition from insurance agents who demanded provisions to protect their turf from bank infiltration.
Hawke said he believes the concerns of the insurance agents can be addressed and bank powers broadened.

"The primary thing that they are concerned about is preserving state regulation over insurance agency activities, and we don't have any problem with that provided ... that it doesn't discriminate against banks," Hawke said.
The Treasury's plan will also have a provision that would allow mutual thrifts, which are owned by depositors rather than shareholders, to continue in that form, he said.
